content: The study by Thornton et al. (2013) compared the use of oxytocin versus no treatment or delayed treatment for slow progress during the first stage of spontaneous labor. The quality of evidence was assessed as very low for critical outcomes, such as Apgar scores below 7 at 5 minutes, due to serious design limitations and the absence of events in the trials. The findings were not pooled due to the lack of events, and the results were deemed inconclusive. In another analysis by Bugg et al. (2013), the early use of oxytocin was compared to delayed use for slow progress in the first stage of labor. For maternal outcomes, the evidence was of moderate quality, showing a reduction of 69 fewer adverse events per 1,000 women, though the confidence interval ranged from 166 fewer to 41 more events. For infant outcomes, the evidence was of low quality, with an estimated reduction of 3 fewer adverse events per 1,000 infants, but the confidence interval crossed the line of no effect. Kenyon et al. (2013) evaluated high-dose versus low-dose oxytocin regimens for labor augmentation. For maternal outcomes, the evidence was of low quality, with 129 fewer adverse events per 1,000 women (confidence interval: 7 fewer to 183 fewer). For infant outcomes, the evidence was very low quality, with 39 fewer adverse events per 1,000 infants (confidence interval: 61 fewer to 12 more). The findings were limited by small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals, and design limitations in the contributing studies. Vogel et al. (2013) investigated the use of titrated oral misoprostol for labor augmentation. For maternal outcomes, the evidence was of low quality, with 77 fewer adverse events per 1,000 women (confidence interval: 172 fewer to 26 more). For infant outcomes, the evidence was very low quality, with 25 more adverse events per 1,000 infants (confidence interval: 9 fewer to 196 more). The results were limited by small sample sizes, few events, and wide confidence intervals. Smyth et al. (2013) examined the use of routine amniotomy alone for treating delays in the first stage of labor. For maternal outcomes, the evidence was very low quality, with 56 fewer adverse events per 1,000 women (confidence interval: 100 fewer to 402 more). For infant outcomes, the evidence was also very low quality, with no significant differences observed. The findings were limited by design flaws, small sample sizes, and the absence of events in some studies. Wei et al. (2013) assessed the combination of early amniotomy and oxytocin for treating delays in the first stage of labor. For maternal outcomes, the evidence was of low quality, with 57 fewer adverse events per 1,000 women (confidence interval: 117 fewer to 183 more). For infant outcomes, the evidence was very low quality, with no significant differences observed. The results were affected by design limitations, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals. Bakker et al. (2013) compared internal versus external tocodynamometry during augmented labor. For maternal outcomes, the evidence was of moderate quality, with 76 more adverse events per 1,000 women (confidence interval: 6 more to 161 more). For infant outcomes, the evidence was of low quality, with 60 more adverse events per 1,000 infants (confidence interval: 19 fewer to 183 more). The findings were limited by design flaws, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals.
